name: Bhutan
summary_text: Bhutan is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression. Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.

sources.title: Bhutan | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021; LGBTIQ organisations can register (though the process is lengthy). No stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; legal gender recognition is unavailable in practice, though authorities previously allowed some changes.

sources.title: Trans women face hurdles in reporting violence - BBSCL
sources.claim_summary: Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): 'Trans women face hurdles in reporting violence' - trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report assaults, family pressure to 'accept it as fate', and laws that 'only cater to men and women'.

sources.title: UNFPA Bhutan | Fostering Awareness: Advancing LGBT+ Rights & Inclusivity in Bhutan
sources.claim_summary: UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness: Advancing LGBT+ Rights & Inclusivity in Bhutan' (March 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign advanced LGBTIQ+ equality among policymakers, parliamentarians and institutions (Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General, Cabinet Secretariat), securing the first direct dialogue between the LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians in Bhutan's history.

sources.title: Bhutan prepares to repeal its anti-gay laws
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (June 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted nearly unanimously (43-1) to repeal the 'unnatural sex' provisions (Sections 213-214, punishable by 1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

sources.title: Bhutan drops its law against sodomy
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2021): Bhutan's Penal Code Amendment Act came into force Feb 17, 2021 - after the upper house reinserted the provision, a joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex'; decriminalisation completed.

sources.title: Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow - BBSCL
sources.claim_summary: Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature: 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow' - the emergence of Bhutan's LGBT community via the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page; profiles of administrators and Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly (who fought to wear a kira to school at 16); notes self-stigma is significant but discrimination 'not very widespread'.

sources.title: Gay in Nirvana: Bhutan’s LGBT Population Emerges from the Shadows
sources.claim_summary: The Daily Beast (Oct 2015): 'Gay in Nirvana' - Bhutan's small LGBT population has experienced very little persecution or violence, but the concept of being gay or trans is 'pretty much unheard of'; no shared language for these identities; lesbianism under-recognised; Karma Dupchen created the first public LGBT outlet (LGBT Bhutan Facebook page) in 2013.
